Area · Core processes

Comparative psychology

What other animals think and feel, and what comparing them with us teaches us.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Comparative psychology studies the behaviour and minds of other species and compares them with ours. It helps us understand where abilities such as memory, learning or cooperation come from, and also to know animals in their own right. Many classic findings in psychology, from Pavlov's conditioning to Köhler's insight, came from studies with animals.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

From the horse that "counted" to the laboratory

In the early twentieth century a Berlin horse called Hans seemed to solve arithmetic problems. In 1907 Oskar Pfungst showed that it was responding to involuntary gestures by its questioners. The case left a rule: always look for the simplest explanation and control the cues we give without meaning to. The biologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan had already formulated a similar principle, "Morgan's canon".

What has been discovered

  • Tool use: in 1960 Jane Goodall observed chimpanzees using twigs to fish out termites. New Caledonian crows make hooks.
  • Self-recognition: in 1970 Gordon Gallup created the mirror test. Great apes, dolphins, Asian elephants and some magpies pass it, although the test has limits.
  • Memory: birds that cache food remember thousands of hiding places for months.
  • Communication: Karl von Frisch deciphered the dance by which bees indicate where food is (Nobel Prize, 1973).
  • Culture: some populations of chimpanzees, whales or birds pass on customs that other groups of the same species lack.

What they don't do

Attempts to teach language to apes, such as Washoe with signs or Kanzi with symbols, showed that they can learn hundreds of signs and combine them, but no complex grammar like human grammar has been seen in them.

Different intelligences

Each species is intelligent for its way of life. Octopuses, with most of their neurons in their arms, open jars and escape from tanks. Dogs understand human pointing better than chimpanzees, probably thanks to thousands of years of living together. Bees can learn concepts such as "same" and "different". Comparing species on a single scale of "intelligence" makes little sense.

Animal cultures

In 1999, Andrew Whiten and other primatologists compared seven chimpanzee populations studied for decades and found dozens of behaviours that varied from group to group with no ecological reason: some cracked nuts with stones and others did not, though they had both nuts and stones. These were passed on through social learning, like human traditions. Since then, cultures have been described in whales, whose songs change and spread from one population to another, and in birds.

Do animals have personality?

Anyone who has had several dogs knows each is different. Research confirms it: in many species, from chimpanzees to octopuses and fish, individuals differ consistently in traits such as boldness, sociability or exploration. Samuel Gosling showed that different keepers agree when rating the same animal's personality, which suggests it is not just a human projection.

Birds that learn to sing

Songbirds such as finches learn their song by imitating an adult during a sensitive period in youth, first babbling and then refining. If they do not hear it in time, their song remains abnormal. The parallel with children learning to speak is so close that songbirds are used as a model to study the biology of language, including the FOXP2 gene.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

Do animals feel?

In 2012 a group of neuroscientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, which stated that many animals, including mammals, birds and some invertebrates such as octopuses, have the neurological substrates of conscious experience. In 2024 the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness called for taking seriously the possibility of experience in fish, insects and crustaceans too.

Research ethics

Harry Harlow's experiments with rhesus monkeys in the 1950s, which separated infants from their mothers, showed the importance of contact and affection, but are now considered unacceptable because of the suffering they caused. Current research follows the principle of the "three Rs": replace, reduce and refine the use of animals.

Comparing without humanising

The primatologist Frans de Waal warned against two errors: attributing human abilities to animals without evidence (anthropomorphism) and denying them any resemblance to us out of prejudice, which he called "anthropodenial". Comparative psychology today tries to design tests suited to each species rather than measuring them by human standards.

Empathy and fairness in animals

In an experiment by Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal (2003), capuchin monkeys given cucumber accepted the exchange until they saw their partner receive grapes: then they refused the cucumber. Other studies describe rats freeing a trapped companion before eating chocolate. Whether this reflects human-like empathy or simpler mechanisms is debated, but it suggests evolutionary roots of fairness and helping.

Belyaev's foxes

In 1959, Soviet geneticist Dmitri Belyaev began breeding silver foxes, selecting in each generation the least aggressive and calmest with people. Within a few decades he had foxes that sought human contact and wagged their tails, and that also had floppy ears, piebald coats and curled tails, traits seen in many domestic animals. The experiment, still running in Novosibirsk, suggests that selecting for tameness alone brings other physical and behavioural changes with it.

Declarations on animal consciousness

In 2012, a group of neuroscientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, stating that many animals, including all mammals, birds and octopuses, possess the neurological substrates of consciousness. In 2024, the New York Declaration went further, calling for the possibility of conscious experience in reptiles, fish and even insects to be taken seriously. These are consensus positions, not proofs, but they influence animal welfare law.
